displayTitle: 2026-07-30 - Transport and Infrastructure Committee - Local Government (Port Companies Accountability) Amendment Bill
topic: Local Government (Port Companies Accountability) Amendment Bill
description: 30 July 2026 | Transport and Infrastructure Committee Local Government (Port Companies Accountability) Amendment Bill Port of Tauranga Limited Leonard Sampson, Chief Executive Maritime Union of New Zealand Inc. Carl Findlay, National Secretary Rob Egan, Consultant Clint Smith, Consultant New Zealand Council of Trade Unions Cory Bourne, Team Leader – Senior Policy Melissa Ansell-Bridges, Secretary Port CEOs Group Ian Bonnar, Executive Director Taxpayers' Union Ray Deacon, Economist NZ Forest Owners Association Elizabeth Heeg, Chief Executive Joseph Brolly, Chief Operating Officer
descriptionSummary: Local Government (Port Companies Accountability) Amendment Bill. Port of Tauranga Limited. Leonard Sampson, Chief Executive

chunks.text: Look, we've got the submissions as read. I don't know if you've seen the other parties' submissions as well that we're considering this morning, because there's a bit of a competition of ideas in there, and we might well ask you questions about what you think about some of their comments. But what I'll do is I'll set the time for 10 minutes.

Sure. And I'll give you a call with four to go if you're still going. Take the submission as read. And we do like asking questions, there's probably quite a few. So, in your hands. Sure. No problem. Well, thank you, and kia ora tātou. Thank you for having me. Leonard Samson, Chief Executive of Port of Tauranga. Look, just from a port perspective, Port of Tauranga, we fundamentally oppose extending the Local Government Informations Act.

Fundamentally, our view is that the existing commercial accountability arrangements are fit for purpose, and that the bill would create unnecessary commercial, legal, and security risks. The application of the LGOIMA incorrectly treats port companies as council-controlled organizations when they are commercially governed businesses.

The purpose of the LGOIMA is to support democratic participation and accountability in local government objectives, and they do not align with the port company's commercial mandate. The commercial mandate of port companies aligns with the Port Companies Act 1998, and it requires ports to operate as successful commercial businesses and provides accountability measures that are suited to that purpose.

This was a deliberate governance model that Parliament intentionally created to commercially govern ports and preserve the agility, confidentiality to promote effective competition in freight markets. Another added complexity for Port of Tauranga is that its listed issuer status as an NZX-listed company with public and private shareholders, we're already subject to significant market disclosure and shareholder obligations.

Moving away from the current arrangements would impact investor confidence. Applying public sector information regimes could disrupt shareholder relationships, commercial confidentiality, and investor confidence. It is also not comparable with other partially publicly owned businesses operating in competitive markets.

For example, Air New Zealand, Mercury Energy, are not subject to the comparable official information regimes. The existing accountability, reporting, audits, and regulatory oversight and shareholder scrutiny already provide significant transparency without the need to extend to further LGOIMA requirements.

And finally, there is no clear or proportionate case. It's not clear from the bill that's evidenced any accountability failure, and it's hard to understand the purposes behind the broad intervention and disproportionate issue that is claimed. That's the basis for my submission, so I don't need to take up the full 10 minutes.

I'm happy to take any questions. Excellent. There's a lot of value in question time. So I'll start with Dan. Hey, thank you, Leonard. Really good to have your submission and before our committee today. As a listed company, I guess there's already a huge amount of disclosure requirements. Can you kind of elaborate for the committee the extent of information requirements that any listed company has to the public and to its shareholders?

Fundamentally, there's a continuous disclosure requirement that means anything that can be considered material, and that material test is significant. So anything that could be considered to have a... And it is a test that could have any influence, whether it be in terms of investor confidence, share price, et cetera, we need to make disclosures.

So even as simple as we are employing a new executive team member, we're just about in the process of looking to make, we need to make that listed issuer disclosure. Any fundamental changes, any new business we secure that could be significant to the port and have an influence flow through to share price, that needs to require a disclosure.

Any change to governance, any new directors. So it's hard to go and list every example because in a lot of cases, it's pretty much everything anyway. It's anything that could be considered to be material. And that material test is not binary and you err on the side of caution because anything can be considered material in a lot of cases.

Yeah, thank you. And maybe a second question, if I can, Mr. Chair, is as part of your requirements, you run annual general meetings. I'm assuming they are robust forums for your shareholders. Is that correct? That's correct. We hold twice a year interim, so we have an interim and a full year investor day analyst briefings. And so providing, making sure, and that's available to all investors.

And so, shareholders have representation at those there. We also hold annual AGMs, and they are very robust, with plenty of time for shareholders to go and participate in terms of questions in advance and be involved in the governance of the port.

Thank you very much. Carlos. Hi. Thank you. I just wonder if this law is passed, what is the extra or additional operational cost will it create? Or how will these changes affect the efficiency and productivity? There's a significant impact to-- I guess, there's a significant administration burden that would be associated with it.

And you would potentially continually be running the test over what's commercially sensitive and what's not. And so, in a lot of cases when you talk about from a port company perspective, the model, it was a deliberate model that was put in place with the Port Companies Act to actually preserve confidentiality and provide effective competition within the freight market. So from a Legoyma perspective, for example, the international shipping lines, all of those type of things, you could find yourself being in significant areas where you're

having to redact a lot of time, things that could be considered commercially sensitive. Just the administration function in itself would be a significant burden on our organization. In terms of impact, in terms of specifically port productivity, I'm not sure. And while we support absolute transparency around the reporting of port productivity figures, this is not the pathway to do that in terms of the Legoyma pathway.

That is something that there's a separate, as you note here, Andy. There's a separate piece of work going on in terms of an inquiry into port company productivity that should be looking to go and address those type of outcomes. But the Legoyma requirement won't have any measurable impact whatsoever in terms of port productivity.

Thank you. I've got a few questions too. Just first of all, because this comes out of the point that you are partially, or all ports are at least partially owned by- Yes... local bodies. The relationship you have with Quayside Holdings, how could you characterize that? Is it active, passive? What is it?

It's an active relationship. It's a very good relationship. I guess what I will say here is the mandate of Quayside, if you like to act as the custodian or the asset owner of regional assets, and with an independent commercial mandate to operate those as intergenerational investment entities, has effectively acted as a buffer between local government, local body politics, if you like, and running a port operation. Quayside fundamentally make our lives a lot easier by having an intermediary

in between the Port of Tauranga and the ultimate shareholder being the regional council. And it allows the Port of Tauranga to focus on running its business, which is actually running a port operational business and doing the best we can in terms of providing services to our customers, and obviously running our business and playing our part in the community.

No, thanks. Are they subject to Legoyma, Quayside? Good question. They will be CCAP potentially. I'm not entirely sure. Okay. It'd be good actually if we can understand that because- I can come back and clarify that for you. Yes. Yeah, because there are a number of holding companies which hold port assets across the country, and other assets as well.

Second area of question I just wanted to ask. In the Port Companies Act, there's the requirement, as you said, and deliberate requirement of the legislation to act as a successful business, and that is the only stipulation there. If you look at the definition of what they usually use definition of successful business, it is not purely commercial. It's a multiplicity of things which includes good customer relations, good relations with community, all that sort of stuff. What's your view of what being a successful business is and is not?

Well, I think yes, a successful organization is more than just the commercial outcomes. But the fact that a commercial is in there, to me indicates that there needs to be a level of capital discipline applied to those businesses, that would be consistent with it being in a private setting. And I guess what I mean to that, that is one area that you have the Auditor General as the auditor for the port companies, and actually holding port companies to account for the capital decisions that they make. And again, another point I want to raise here,

as a listed entity is we have those capital disciplines forced upon us by being a listed entity. We make poor capital decisions, we see it in our share price the very next day. We're accountable to our shareholders at any point in time as and when we make those decisions. And as I mentioned before, with the continuous disclosure requirements, any significant capital decisions will trigger those requirements.

Cool. And look, I wanted to ask one other question because, certainly in our inquiry and discussions, there is one particular project which you've got on the go, which I think we're all vitally interested in, which is the Stella Passage project. Well, first of all, I'm interested in how you're getting on, but I'm also interested in how that project would be affected were it subject to Legoyma.

It's hard to know the nature of the-- It would open up to all realms of different types of scrutiny and questioning, and some of which you're going through a process, whether it be an environmental process and now in a fast-track panel process that there's a lot of discussions that are covered under, I guess, in some cases privileged.

So I'm not sure. But frankly, I don't think it helps that process at all, because I'm not sure what additional transparency you'd have. Just to answer your first part of your question, which was how are we going in that process? We just spent three days In a hearing by the fast-track panel, and so we await a decision by September.

Excellent. I wish you well. Thank you. Thank you. Any other questions, colleagues? No. Thank you. Look, what I was looking for there was just to understand whether you thought that would intrude even more into that process. And look, I will ask tame- I think inevitably it would do, because you- But without understanding the nature of the types of questions that will get asked, inevitably it would.

That would further go and potentially delay it. I've got a question. Okay. Tracy's got one other question. Just because you've raised that. And then I've got one. Yeah. It's certainly my understanding that the bill doesn't change any of your existing reporting obligations. It just adds something extra. So under the Auditor-General and the Companies Act, and all of the ways in which you already assume you have public accountability, do you have to report on environmental effects, on workplace practices, on any kind of relationship with public owners?

I say that because I noted that you say that you describe yourself as a privately owned business, acknowledging the fact that you are 54% owned by the public essentially. So do you already disclose or report on those other factors- Yes... or are those the ones- Yeah, we do. Yeah, absolutely. We disclose annually in our annual report, we'll always disclose our health and safety metrics. We'll disclose...

We've got extensive environmental metrics that we've developed over the past years. And again, I guess from our perspective, there are obviously more and more in terms of ESG requirements, and obviously we're subject to climate related disclosures as a listed entity. And so again, that brings a whole another layer of transparency and reporting requirements that are mandated.

But even in the ones that are not mandated, we already provide all of those in terms of health and safety, workplace reporting. We provide all of that information today and that level of transparency. Right. Thank you. And look, the other question I was going to ask, because it is one that we've traversed elsewhere, is the issues around transparency of charges.

So whether it's gate charges, port charges, whatever it might be. We've heard some sort of light touch, com type arrangements, which some ports essentially say they subject themselves to already. Have you got a view on how best those charging regimes might be made as transparent as possible?

Where you would go, where you wouldn't go. I guess you go back to the Port Companies Act that requires to operate as a commercial successful business. I think if you looked at the port sector across the board, there's not that many port companies in the entire country that are operating what you would consider successful commercial businesses.

There are a number of port companies that are operating in negative free cash flow. So from a net perspective, I'm not sure that there's a fundamental issue there. But port companies, we have regular publishing of our tariffs are available on our website.

I'm just not sure in terms of if your question then relates to the transparency, are they available? Yes, they're publicly available at any point in time, but there's always a process that you go through with our customers in those discussions, and I suspect each port company as its own business needs to go and undertake those processes.

Yeah. Okay. No, that's really helpful. Thank you, Leonard. Really appreciate the time. Really appreciate the submission and wish you well for September. Thank you very much. Thank you for having me. Thanks, Leonard. Thank you. Cheers. Bye. Right. Okay, now we've got the Maritime Union of New Zealand who are also on Zoom.

Morning Clint, Carl, and Rob. Morning. Good to see you there. I'm getting an echo there. Anyway, we've got you down for 10 minutes. You can take the submission as read. Anything you want to highlight, really appreciate that. There'll be plenty of questions, and I think there'll be some cross-referencing of questions between the various submissions, so I don't know if you've read the other submissions that we've got in front of us at the moment, but each of you is challenging each other's positions, so it's all good.

So we look forward to what you've got to say. I'll give you a call with four minutes to go. We may go a little bit of a stretch over, but, we'll try not to. But, yeah, in your hands. Excellent. Well, thank you very much for having us. We appreciate it. Really appreciate the time and being here. Yeah, as you say, our submission speaks for itself and, I won't hold up too much of the time, just yet.

I'll hand it over to Rob and Clint to go through it in a bit more finer detail and chip in a bit later on. Thank you. Thank you, Carl. So our view is that ports are strategic national assets. But despite being fully or partially council owned and key nodes in our transport network, there is input from the normal transparency that applies to other strategic transport assets like NZTA.

Even privately owned asset holders like electricity lines companies and airports are subject to more oversight through the Commerce Commission that doesn't apply to seaports. Responding to some of the issues raised by the previous submitter, not all ports are listed on the NZX, and the transparency requirements of the NZX are fundamentally different from official information legislation.

As he himself alluded to, with his claims that complying with official information disclosure would be burdensome. Now, responding to that point, I'm a school board chair. We're a small school. We are subject to disclosure under the Official Information Act. We have to do that.

If a small school can manage it, I think a large port can. The costs are relatively minor and transparency is important. The issues with the The lack of transparency in the current regime was exemplified by Ports of Auckland's lack of transparency during the 2012 lockout and during their disastrous automation project.

This bill is timely because as the committee has recently heard during the ports inquiry, New Zealand is moving towards a hub and spoke model port organization where international vessels will service only a few key ports and freight will be transported between those ports and regional spokes by coastal vessels. That is going to happen whether it is a government-led process or imposed on us by international shipping lines.

A hub and spoke model to be successful for New Zealand will require a national port strategy and greater coordination of investment between ports and with government to ensure we have the infrastructure where we need it and that we need. That won't be possible if ports continue to act as if they're simple, private, isolated identities like the corner shop rather than the strategic assets in our transport network that they are.

So this bill will help put New Zealand in a better place for the reality that we are facing in the port sector as we move towards a hub and spoke model. The one amendment that MANZ has suggested would be to ensure that private operators are also covered by the disclosure regime. The prospect of privatization of port operations, as is currently being proposed for Lyttelton, should not become a loophole to avoid transparency and stymie coordination.

And we see that being a real risk that the transparency that's needed and that this bill would help to accomplish would be stymied if we see private operators exempted from it. Thank you. Thank you. You good for questions? Yes. Okay, cool. Right. Questions, colleagues. Tracy.

Thanks. Thank you, and thank you for your submission. Can you give me some examples of what sort of specific information that you've been unable to obtain from ports that you would have liked to have? Well, the Ports of Auckland automation process was a huge example of where hundreds of millions of dollars of what was ultimately ratepayers' money was wasted by port management who had this-- They wanted to de-unionize the port, and they had this vainglorious idea of themselves.

During that process, the union was largely shut out. De-unionizing the port was part of the goal of the automation process, and councilors also found it hard to get information out of the port what was happening. Our belief is that if there had been greater transparency during that automation process, then the alarm bells would've been able to be sounded much earlier, before all that money was wasted, before the lives of workers were lost.

Yeah. I've got an example of actually being at a hearing with the council, where elected councilors were asking the CEO at the time, during the dispute in 2012, some questions, and he just kept hiding behind the corporate veil, saying it was sensitive information that he couldn't share because it had implications to the company. And as we all know the result of what that carry on did to the port.

And so it really has to stop, this covering up and hiding behind that corporate veil. The community should be able to ask questions and get straight answers. There's got to be some accountability. That's what we're after. And I don't think it's necessarily just the community either in discussions.

We talked about this during the ports inquiry and discussions we had with the Infrastructure Commission last year. They also described difficulty mapping in terms of getting the information to map what is effectively incredibly vital infrastructure. So that speaks to the need to plan and, as Clint said, the fact that lack of transparency stymies the ability to plan at a national level.

Yeah. Can I ask two questions? The first one of them is, the Port of Auckland, obviously, who you focused on, because I know obviously the history there, is not subject to the same kind of disciplines that the NZX were put on that Port Taranaki was just talking about. If the same discipline were required, anything that's commercially significant and obviously the investment that was being made and the automation would've absolutely been in that category, so would any risks to that associated with that. That would make that actually

ironically more transparent than it was by the looks of it. Would that be fair? I'm not advocating for a second for privatization, but what I am wondering aloud about is whether in fact if that same discipline was there for the non-privatized, the fully publicly owned companies, whether that would actually make a difference.

Well, obviously there is greater transparency, but it's a particular kind of transparency. This bill would allow greater discourse, greater inquiry. We don't see that the disclosures that you get on the NZX are necessarily completely aligned with the disclosure that you would need, for instance, in making a national assessment across all ports.

It is better, but it's not necessarily fit for purpose. It's a sort of halfway measure or a tool with a different purpose. And that takes me to the other question I was going to ask, which is, we've certainly had quite a number of conversations around the port inquiry, which have gone to the transparency for things like charging regimes, et cetera, investment regimes and so on.

Whether the Commerce Commission has a light touch or a heavier touch oversight of ports is, I think, a live question that's been raised with us. What it seems is that the LGOIMA, I'm well aware of from a local government point of view, is exceedingly intrusive. Possibly more than anybody actually realizes who's made submissions, because I've been on the other end of it, I know how intrusive it is.

But at the moment we've got such a light touch, in your view anyway, that you're not getting the information that's needed. Is there a halfway house, I guess is what I'm asking you. And it may be through a range of different pieces of legislation.

Yeah. You're right that the Commerce Commission, if they had powers over the seaports, could require disclosure of information that's not publicly disclosable now. That's not the question that's in front of us. Right. We see that there'll be real benefits to this, particularly as we move towards the hub and spoke model. So, that's our focus now.

Okay, cool. Julianne. Oh, sorry. It's worth noticing that in the LGOIMA there are still reasonable protections for commercial sensitivity and the like. It's not open slather. Yeah. I know how it works. Julianne. Kia ora. Thank you so much for your submission.

I guess I just wanted to ask, do you think it would be surprising that those organizations would show up to the select committee and say, "Oh, no, we can't do this. This would be a bad thing." Or is that something that we should expect, and be a little more understandable that they're defending their position to not have to comply with something, however, there's still a good case for it?

Yeah. I'd say that the port's position is not surprising, that they'd be opposed to greater transparency. I think as the previous submitter showed, the ethos of the ports tends to be that they're just private companies, just the same as the corner dairy, the same as a factory making widgets.

Our view is that they are not. They are strategic assets that all of them have some level of public ownership, and they are vital to New Zealand's economic future. We are moving towards this hub and spoke model, and they are each crucial nodes in that hub and spoke, whether they'll be spokes or hubs. So, in our view, transparency is vital.

But it's not surprising that their view accords to how they view themselves. Cool. Look, thank you very much. Really appreciate it, and also really appreciate all of the discussions through the inquiry process as well. It's been most helpful to get all the input we've had. Thank you.

Thank you very much. Thanks, man. You're welcome. Enjoy the rest of the day. Okay. Then we've got the NZCTU. Who are also on there. Good morning. Good morning. Good morning. Lovely to see you there. Thank you. So, I'll just clear that. We've got your submission, which you can take as read.

You've got 10 minutes. I'll give you a call with four to go, because we do like asking questions, as you've obviously heard. And so, in your hands. Very good. Well, thank you very much. Tēnā koutou katoa, and thank you for the opportunity to speak to the select committee on our submission on the Local Government Ports Accountability Bill.

I'm Melissa Ransom-Bridges. I'm the Secretary of the New Zealand Council of Trade Unions, and joining me is Corey Bourne, who is in our policy team as a senior policy advisor. We represent over 32 affiliated unions, including MUNZ, who you just heard from. And also, the RMTU, who I understand has also submitted on this bill.

And just to start off, we'd like to begin by saying that we endorse and support the points made in their submissions. Collectively, we represent over 370,000 working people across Aotearoa, New Zealand. And we also acknowledge Te Tiriti o Waitangi as the founding document of Aotearoa, and represent over 60,000 kaimahi Maori through our affiliated unions as well.

So we support this bill. We see it as a modest and practical and also an important step to bring port companies into the same accountability framework as other council-controlled organizations. Ports are publicly owned and publicly connected critical infrastructure, and decisions about them can have major consequences for workers, for local communities, for regional economies, supply chains, iwi and hapū, and also for the environment. These decisions should therefore be made with appropriate transparency, accountability, and

also, importantly for us, regard to good employment practice. We consider that this bill helps achieve that without undermining any commercial role of port companies. I'm going to hand over now to Corey to go through our submission in a bit more detail. And also obviously for even more detail, we defer to MUNZ and RMTU, who have a particularly good understanding of the issues at play in this legislation. Thank you.

Now, Kia ora, select committee . As Mel opened with, the accountability and transparency critical to port companies' social license to operate. They operate and occupy significant public infrastructure on public land, public assets, and they are delivering essential services. I'm sure you'll probably hear this a lot today, but we know that 99% of the country's international trade by volume comes through our ports.

So we're not here to dispute that they're not cr-- they are critical infrastructure, both regionally and nationally. The scale and impact of their operations are very diverse. So they're large employers in their local communities. And with port land use on the waterfront, it means there are relevant environmental and cultural factors, and therefore a number of different interests in the governance of these assets.

We think the bill introduces some fairly minor changes that will help with the accountability to those local interests, and note that submission of demands around ensuring that those privately operated ports aren't out of scope of those provisions, too. We would suggest that this bill isn't creating new obligations out of nowhere, applies those existing understood rules from the LGOIMA that other entities already work within. We're not looking at special treatment for the ports, just to remove that historical exemption that's seen them left out.

And as we heard from Munz, that there is those withholding grounds built in. Andy, you were saying that you feel like it is quite intrusive, but there are grounds there around withholding information and if there's too much to disclose, those protections are there, we would suggest.

Secondly, just want to talk briefly to the importance of supporting good work that this bill seeks to do. Unsurprisingly, we're widely focused on supporting good work, which is mahi that has a lasting positive impact on the worker, the employer, the wider community. Good work means, among other things, fair wages, health and safe work, productive and cooperative workplaces, and meaningful and fulfilling work that contributes to society.

We are therefore supportive of this bill to help port companies and their workforces realize good work. They're more and more understanding these days that businesses operate beyond a narrow view of profit margins and the operations impact the workforces and the communities that they are based in. Again, suggesting that this bill is just bringing ports into that already established framework and not trying to overhaul the regulatory framework around them, but support them to be locally beneficial and accountable operations. My background's health and safety, so I'm going to focus on

that as one aspect of good work. Port work is physically demanding, it's high risk, often involves shift work and other forms of work like that. It means that we see some serious health and safety issues, fatigue, moving plant and vehicles, rail operations, working at heights, among others. These have fatal consequences if governance is poor.

Alongside worker engagement, good governance is the critical element of successful workplace health and safety. In our written sub, we highlighted the turnaround of the operations at Ports of Auckland as something that regulatory settings should support. Ports of Auckland had that horrendous health and safety record with some severe failings that led to worker fatalities and then first HSWA conviction of an officer.

But that turnaround, that was bringing good governance and the workforce of Ports of Auckland together and saw the port significantly increase its productivity, and at the same time dramatically increasing employee engagement. So we think those are the kind of settings that regulatory settings should try and support and practice. And while the bill, we say it's only light touch, but we think it will slightly move the needle in that way.

And just want to make the final point that good employment is not in competition with commercial performance. In fact, it's the opposite that's often true, where productive businesses are those that work with their employees, they're safe, and they are productive. Beyond the employment sphere, we think it's important for ports to demonstrate social and environmental responsibility by having regard to the interests of the community in which they operate.

We think regulatory settings should support the ports to work with their workforce, their local communities, including iwi and hapū, to mitigate their impacts on the environment and continue to maintain their social license to operate. On that basis, we recommend that- We've got about three and a half minutes left. Just finishing. Final sentence. Oh We are recommending that the bill passes for that balanced approach to transparency and accountability of these critical assets and for supporting the ports to be good employers for everyone's

benefit. Thank you for your time. Thank you both. Colleagues, looking for questions. Tracy. Thank you. Just going back to health and safety, given that it's a particular penchant of yours, can you give me any practical kind of examples of how having better direct access to information around health and safety could help, not just identify, but perhaps prevent accidents or encourage better ways of working?

Is there an end game here? I think that when we're talking about health and safety, we're talking around that good employment governance piece. But to the point around information sharing, that is a critical element of good health and safety as well, right? When you're engaging the workers and they need to know what the decision-making processes are, what the issues are that we're actually trying to address. So having as much information as possible is helpful when you're collaborating on health and safety responses to things

on the ports. Okay, thank you. Two questions from me, if I can. First one of them is, you've talked about in your written submission that at, two, the profit margins are the sole concern. Now, I note that the Port Companies Act actually says operate a successful business.

Yeah. As I understand, there is no legal Definition of successful business, but it's generally accepted to be much more than profit. It includes health and safety, community, environment, all sorts of other things. You're making a statement there- Right... which I'm not sure is entirely true.

But would it be helpful to actually say that those things are, in one way or the other, they are legally what we expect a successful business to do, as opposed to just we assume that that's what people think it means? Yeah, I think so. And in the context of the introduction there, that's around maybe some of the framework of setting those reforms of the '80s, where profit margins were the sole driver, not necessarily that the ports only have those. But I take your point.

Things might have evolved since then. Yes. Yeah. I'm saying it's a relic of the time that they are outside that scope. So would it be helpful to be a bit more explicit about that expectation that successful business does not just mean a financial bottom line, but more than that? Yes, I would agree with that. Okay, cool. Thank you.

And then the other question I had was just, you've made the comment also in your written submission, significant public expenditure has been made to develop and maintain these built environments, i.e. the ports themselves. I just wondered perhaps to what degree that's true, that it's significant public investment's been put in.

It might have been a long, long time ago, but I don't know whether, if you like, ratepayers have been putting money into ports for quite a long time. I think it's been basically built on the business. The one question I'd have on that context would be Port of Lyttelton, which if they do a big development, the ratepayer will be significantly involved in that discussion.

Mm-hmm. But as a general statement, is that necessarily the case? Or is the fact that it's been built on the business of the customers effectively have been the ones that have been paying for it rather than the ratepayer? I think as you point out, Eddie, it might be a little bit of both- Yeah... the original setup. But then there are situations, as you say, where expansion or changing in operations, there might be a question of ratepayer input there as well.

Okay. One for us to think about. Look, really appreciate that. I'll just check. I don't see any other questions, so thank you very much. Really appreciate it. Thanks for your time. Appreciate it. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Okay, and now we move to in-person for the last three we've got. So we have first up, Ian. Welcome.

Morning, everyone. And congratulations again on being the new port CEO, sir. Oh, thank you very much. Executive director. Thanks for the opportunity, and hopefully something for the committee. So again, take the submission as it is. We've got 10 minutes. I'll give you a call with four to go. All right. Thank you. If we can scrape it over, then we scrape it over. We'll try not to. All right. Good morning, everybody. Mr.

Chairman and members of the committee, my name is Ian Bonner, and I am the Executive Director of the Port CEOs Group. Thank you for the opportunity to appear before you today. Our written submission was developed following consultation with the CEOs of all 13 commercial port companies represented by this organization.

While those ports differ significantly in ownership, scale, and commercial model, there was unanimous agreement on the position before you today. Rather than repeat the written submission, I would like to briefly summarize why the Port CEOs Group does not support the bill in its current form, and then propose an alternative path forward. Our concerns can be summarized in three points.

First, as you've already heard, Parliament deliberately established the port companies to operate as commercial businesses, and designed an accountability regime around that. Exclusion from LogOIMA was not an oversight. It was intentional and reflects the reality of port operations. Secondly, and I want to be very clear here, the ports are not resistant to transparency.

We support the objective of strong public accountability, but we do not believe the bill has demonstrated that the existing accountability framework is materially failing. And thirdly, should it be concluded that even greater transparency is desirable, we do not believe this legislation will deliver the transparency or public understanding you are seeking.

So I'd like to begin with the legislative context. The current framework is not an accident. The Port Companies Act states that the principal objective of every port company is to operate as a successful business. So ports compete with each other for freight, they compete for shipping services, they negotiate commercial contracts, make large long-term infrastructure investments, and they increasingly compete internationally as part of global supply chains.

Parliament recognized that publicly owned ports could remain publicly accountable while operating under commercial disciplines, rather than as extensions of local government administration. This bill would alter that balance. In our view, such a change should be supported by a clearly identified policy problem and evidence that the existing framework is no longer achieving Parliament's original intent.

We are not persuaded that that threshold has been met. The port sector fully accepts that public accountability matters. The question is not whether ports should be accountable, they already are. As our written submission sets out, ports already operate within extensive accountability arrangements through shareholder oversight, company law, environmental regulation, health and safety regulation, maritime regulation, continuous disclosure obligations for listed companies, and a range of existing public reporting requirements.

If you consider that there are genuine accountability gaps, we would welcome that discussion. But we do not believe that the bill clearly identifies where the existing framework has failed or why changing the model established by Parliament is the appropriate response More information does not necessarily produce more transparency.

Its purpose is to improve accountability and public understanding. The committee should therefore ask not simply whether the bill might produce more information, it should ask whether it will produce better understanding.

Legoyma provides access to information held by individual organizations, but many of the questions you raised are not questions about individual port companies, they're questions about the freight system as a whole.
